articles.title: Unmanned systems take center stage at Turkish Ateş Serbest military demonstration
articles.snippet: The highlight of the exercise may have been the Turkish military showing off a new drone for the first time: Turkish Aerospace Industries’ Ayaz, a turbojet-powered one-way attack unmanned aerial vehicle.
articles.full_text:
ANKARA — Turkish F-16 fighter jets flew overhead, dropping bombs perfectly aimed at targets below, the ground shaking as journalists and visitors alike watched on from a distance.
Drones buzzed around conducting missions while smoke plumes erupted from every direction as targets were hit. If it weren’t for the civilians walking around taking notes the scene could easily be mistaken for a battlefield. Instead, all of this took place at the Ateş Serbest exercise in Ankara earlier this month.
Translated as “Free Fire” in Turkish, the exercise, which took place at the General Nahit Şenoğul Firing and Exercise Area, showed off layered live-fire capabilities, air defense platforms, fighter jet strike capabilities and more. (Breaking Defense, like other outlets, accepted travel and accommodations from the Turkish Ministry of Defense to cover the event.)
The exercise aims to improve “coordination of fire support between forces,” to “introduce weapons and systems in the inventory and demonstrate the effect of the weapons on the target,” and “to provide deterrence” through the firepower, according to a brochure distributed to journalists by the Turkish Ministry of Defense.
At the forefront of the exercise were unmanned systems, many of which were also viewed in various stages of production by Breaking Defense during a series of industry visits to Aselsan, Turkish Aerospace, Asfat, MKE and Roketsan. In discussions during those visits, company officials across the board emphasized the importance of unmanned systems both for Turkey’s domestic use and as potential export items.
The highlight of the exercise may have been the Turkish military showing off a new drone for the first time: Turkish Aerospace Industries’ Ayaz, a turbojet-powered one-way attack unmanned aerial vehicle.
Breaking Defense saw a nearly completed Ayaz drone on the assembly line. On that same tour, the company also showed off its Super Simsek UAV on the assembly line. The exercise marked the first time the Super Simsek flew with a warhead after its maiden voyage in 2023.
Both the Ayaz and the Super Simsek “successfully conducted dive attacks and struck their targets during the Atış Serbest exercise, marking their first use with live warheads,” a company official told Breaking Defense during the tour.
Another highlight was watching as 20 Kargu one-way attack drones from STM hit their targets simultaneously. The drones, which flew in swarms, shared real-time data with each other and the operator, and when they got closer to the enemy infantry, the platforms were divided into two categories and headed towards their targets.
The unmanned systems aren’t just used for attacking. On the far right side of the exercise, a Puhu UAV, which is produced by DASAL Aviation and Space Technologies, was seen carrying medical aid to help snipers injured in the simulated battlefield. A Palem unmanned ground vehicle provided medical evacuations as well.
Throughout the exercise, soldiers used artificial intelligence to control the unmanned systems as well as conduct intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions. For example, battlefield information collected from ISR drones was gathered at the Mobile Command System to help soldiers decide whether to strike or not.
As drones become a more prominent part of the warfield, countries have been giving more attention to developing counter-drone systems — and Turkey is no exception. Drones were used heavily in the recent war between Iran, US and Israel where Shahed UAVs were used extensively by Iran to strike neighboring Gulf states. The US also used one-way attack drones similar to the Shahed, dubbed the Low-Cost Unmanned Combat Attack System, to attack targets in Iran. Further, it used unmanned surface vessels to monitor the Gulf seas and to attack Iranian ports.
Other scenarios carried out during the exercise included Atak helicopters flying overhead, releasing flares and firing Cirit and UMTAS missiles.
Factory Tours
The industrial tours did not result in any new revelations of technology about to break through, but taken as a whole, gave the sense that Turkey’s defense companies are trying to meet the global demand, both domestically and for export. Here are a few notes:
- At Roketsan’s factory, Cirit and UMTAS missiles were shown moving through the assembly line, starting from small parts and finishing as completed missiles. There were also models of the company’s other weapons on display. A company official told Breaking Defense that the latest conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have led to doubling production of missiles, on average, although they did not provide more detailed numbers.
- Counter-drone systems seem a priority for a number of companies. At the exercise, Aselsan’s Ejderha microwave platforms and Gokberk laser systems could be seen shooting down drones. Additionally, MKE’s Tolga. which is a short-range air defense system, could be seen striking targets, with drones falling out of the sky leaving a black trail in their wake.
- At Aselsan’s factory, Breaking Defense saw the Gokberk system sitting completed in the final assembly line, looking as if it was ready to be delivered to a customer. However, no comment was made about what the customer may be. The factory also had air defense systems in two colors — a dark green camouflage, and a yellow camouflage, the latter of which company officials said were for unspecified Middle East customers.
- The tour also included a visit to ASFAT, a Turkish state-owned defense contractor. The firm operates twenty seven military factories and ten naval shipyards across Turkey. Company officials said that the firm has started building the first TF200 guided missile destroyer, Turkey’s ambitious air defense destroyer project.
- At the tour of ASFAT, helicopters from different origins at different stages of refurbishment and MRO could be seen. That meant an unusual sight: Russian built MI-17 helicopters used by the Janderma (armed general law enforcement organization) were sitting next to US-built Sikorsky S-70 and French Cougar H215 helicopters, used by the military.
- As Breaking Defense previously reported, TAI has completed a second production line of its Anka 3 unmanned vehicle.

articles.title: GDIT announces Amy Johnson as new president
articles.snippet: Johnson replaces longtime president Amy Gilliland, who was let go from the company earlier this month after almost a decade of leading the business unit.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT) has a new leader, with company veteran Amy Johnson announced today as incoming president.
Johnson replaces longtime president Amy Gilliland, who was let go from the company earlier this month after almost a decade of leading the business unit. Paul Nedzbala has been serving as acting president in the interim.
“Amy has a proven track record of leading teams to solve complex and highly technical challenges for our customers,” said Phebe Novakovic, the outgoing CEO of General Dynamics, in the announcement. “I am confident that her dynamic leadership, operational rigor and deep commitment to our values and culture will deliver value to our customers, employees and shareholders.”
According to the press release, Johnson is a 27-year veteran of General Dynamics Mission Systems. She was most recently vice president and general manager for Space, Cyber and Intelligence, and has background experience “across cybersecurity, defense electronics, space and intelligence systems.”
Johnson will begin her role as president on Nov. 3.
One of the biggest players in federal IT, GDIT provides critical cyber, software and networking tools to both the military and civilian sector agencies ranging from enterprise to tactical edge applications. The capabilities enable secure communications, full-spectrum cyber operations and monitoring of threats to networks.

articles.title: Space Force reveals first 6 ‘operational’ contracts for civil reserve support in space monitoring
articles.snippet: Space Systems Command officials said the contracts are an initial step for the Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative, and don’t address the thornier issues of US rights to deny other customers service or reimbursement for satellites lost in a conflict.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Space Force has awarded what the service calls the first “operational” contracts under its still-nascent Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative to six space monitoring firms, Space Systems Command (SSC) announced.
The contracts are short term and designed to test military demand while the command’s Commercial Space Office (COMSO) continues to wrestle with thorny legal issues that have bedeviled the program from its launch in 2023.
The six new contracts — issued to Australian firm EOS Space Systems, Canada’s NorthStar Earth and Space, InTrack Radar, Anduril (via its acquisition of ExoAnalytic), Slingshot Aerospace, and LeoLabs — are worth a total of $1.37 million, an SSC spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
CASR is the Space Force’s planned version of the Civil Reserve Air Fleet (CRAF) for leveraging commercial airlines to support military logistics operations when needed, managed by US Transportation Command (TRANSCOM). The concept is that commercial space firms could be called upon in wartime to surge delivery of satellite-derived capabilities.
According to SSC’s Thursday press release, the contracts were let through the “General Services Administration contract framework” used by the Joint Commercial Operations cell to buy commercial data and services. Industry sources who have received similar contracts from the JCO cell have said they tend to run for no more than six months.
The new contracts follow COMSO’s March 2025 award of $1.1 million in three-month pilot contracts to four unnamed companies, first reported by Breaking Defense. Those awards were designed to test out the contracting processes and the CASR framework agreement for interested firms, rather than provide operational data.
According to reports by Air & Space Forces Magazine and Space News, COMSO head Col. Tim Tremillo told reporters during the annual Space Industry Days conference held Oct. 19-22 in Los Angeles that the initial operational awards were meant to provide a short-term boost in space domain awareness data, with the idea that these initial contracts would allow the service to judge military demand. He also made it clear that he expects the CASR program to expand both to more companies and more mission areas.
However, given the small dollar values and short contract duration of the new contracts, it is hard to see how companies will be enticed to join up, said Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“It will be hard for companies to build capacity and capability at scale for use during a crisis if they aren’t paid to do so today. Companies otherwise will not make investments for infrastructure that sits unused and idle, ready for on-demand use, if they are not compensated to build and also maintain that surge capability. Companies do not build extra capacity for sport—it costs money,” he told Breaking Defense today.
Meanwhile, COMSO has yet to develop contractual arrangements that deal with key legal and financial issues that are critical to enticing commercial space companies to join CASR.
The first issue revolves around when and if the US government will have the right to turn off a CASR partner’s services to other customers during a conflict ― a power often referred to as “shutter control.” Companies worry that they could be accused of breach of contract by existing customers if that right were exercised by Washington, and that potential customers (particularly foreign governments) will be scared off.
The second outstanding issue is the question of whether the Pentagon will be willing to indemnify partner firms against financial losses whose satellites are damaged or destroyed during a conflict.

articles.title: Kyiv eyes purchase of planned ICEYE, Nokia ‘sovereign’ communication sats
articles.snippet: The letter of intent comes on the heels of the political dust up between US President Donald Trump and Elon Musk over a US move to throttle Ukraine’s Starshield access that has all but grounded the countries military drones in its war with Russia.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON ― Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) has signed a letter of intent with Finnish firms ICEYE and Nokia to explore development of “sovereign” communications satellites as Kyiv seeks greater control over critical comms infrastructure.
“Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security. We must all rely on capabilities that we can control. The Letter of Intent between the Ministry of Defense, ICEYE, and Nokia is an important step in this direction,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement provided to Breaking Defense today.
“I thank Finland and the Prime Minister of Finland for their consistent support. We value partners who not only help Ukraine, but also work with us to build Europe’s long-term security,” he added.
The agreement was announced Thursday during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s visit to Kyiv. It comes amid uncertainty over Ukraine’s ability to use SpaceX’s Starshield military satellites for drone operations following a US move last week to throttle back the network’s speed — resulting in an ongoing political blame game over responsibility between President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.
Zelenskyy told ABC News today that, despite assurances from Trump that the slowdown had been reversed, Ukraine’s access speeds remained limited.
ICEYE and Nokia announced their partnership Oct. 1 to “develop secure, sovereign and high-performance broadband low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications systems for governments, supporting missions from defense and border security to emergency services and disaster response,” according to a joint press release.
The companies said government customers would have “ownership and control of the satellites, ground segment and terminals,” with the first satellite planned for liftoff in 2028.
Kyiv’s letter of intent marks the first expression of interest in the joint effort, although it falls short of an actual order.
“The LOI with the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine is an expression of intent and does not imply an ordering of any system for Ukraine,” an ICEYE spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
Under the partnership, ICEYE will provide the satellite platform underpinning the joint effort, with the spokesperson explaining that the firm has developed a “flexible platform now being used in satellite communications.”
Nokia will contribute “secure networking technologies” onboard the spacecraft, according to the joint press release.
“Together, the companies will integrate satellites, ground infrastructure and ruggedized end-user terminals to extend ICEYE’s sovereign intelligence from space business model to satellite communications,” the joint press release said.
Based in Helsinki, Nokia provides telecommunications infrastructure, networking capabilities and technologies related to the “internet-of-things.”
ICEYE, headquartered in Espoo, primarily operates synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging satellites and has been expanding both its sales and satellite production capabilities across Europe. The new partnership with Nokia is the company’s first move into SATCOM capabilities.
ICEYE has also been a vocal supporter of Ukraine during its years-long war with Russia. The company recently faced a security concern in orbit when a highly maneuverable Russian Cosmos bird closely approached one of the company’s spacecraft, raising concerns about potentially dangerous on-orbit maneuvers.

articles.title: Ukraine disputes Musk's claims of Starlink misuse as military connectivity restored
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Saturday that Starlink and Starshield connectivity had been restored.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine disputes Musk's claims of Starlink misuse as military connectivity restored
Ukraine's leadership rejected Elon Musk's accusations that its military had misused Starlink's satellite internet service to carry out offensive drone strikes, as Kyiv announced that restrictions disrupting critical military communications had been lifted.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Saturday that Starlink and Starshield connectivity had been restored, with military monitoring systems recording stable connections on equipment exceeding 400 kilometers per hour.
The announcement followed nearly two weeks of disruptions that forced Ukrainian troops to cancel some combat missions and complicated drone operations, reconnaissance and frontline logistics.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Saturday that the restrictions had been lifted, saying connectivity had returned to the levels needed for military operations.
"This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shahed drones," Zelensky said, thanking the United States and other partners for helping resolve the issue.
The apparent resolution came amid a public dispute between Musk and Ukrainian officials over whether Kyiv had misused the satellite service. Musk accused Ukraine's military Saturday of using commercial Starlink terminals to conduct offensive drone strikes, which he said violated the company's rules.
"Ukraine's military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people," Musk wrote on X.
He distinguished commercial Starlink from Starshield, a military-focused version of SpaceX's satellite communications service that he said was controlled by the U.S. government.
"Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them," Musk said.
Ukrainian officials and military advisers disputed his claim, arguing that technical restrictions made it impossible to use commercial Starlink terminals for the drone missions Musk described.
Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist who previously advised the country's defense minister, said a registration system introduced in February required all satellite terminals operating on moving platforms to be connected to the military Starshield service.
"Using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible," Sternenko said, adding that Ukraine had not violated the service's terms.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as "Flash," also rejected Musk's allegations, saying commercial Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine were limited to speeds of 70 to 90 kilometers per hour and did not work on Russian territory.
Those restrictions, he said, prevented Ukrainian forces from using commercial terminals to conduct medium- or long-range drone strikes.
The Starshield restrictions, introduced without warning in mid-October, disrupted connectivity on moving vehicles and drones, causing satellite terminals to lose their connections at higher speeds.
The problems were particularly concerning for Ukraine's efforts to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, which require Ukrainian interceptor drones to travel at high speeds while maintaining reliable communications.
According to a Sunday report by the Institute for the Study of War, Ukraine's interception rate against Russian jet-powered drones declined from 77% to approximately 74% between Oct. 14 and 24, when Starshield was experiencing disruptions.
The researchers said Ukraine maintained a relatively high interception rate despite the restrictions. The figures do not establish whether the connectivity problems directly caused the decline.
It remains unclear who ordered the speed restrictions.
Musk previously said Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the U.S. government and that decisions about speed limits and permitted uses rested with the U.S. military and ultimately President Donald Trump.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Trump had ordered Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions after becoming frustrated that satellite connectivity remained capped at approximately 160 kilometers per hour. Trump denied having spoken to Musk about the issue but said he might intervene if the problems persisted.
The disruption came amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington, including disagreements over Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure and the Trump administration's efforts to pursue a diesel trade agreement with Moscow.
In an interview with Piers Morgan earlier this week, Zelensky said he felt personally betrayed by Trump over the restrictions, accusing Washington of abandoning a crucial partner more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.
Musk, meanwhile, defended SpaceX's role in supporting Ukraine, saying Starlink had been essential to the country's defense since the beginning of the invasion. He warned that Ukraine remained heavily dependent on the satellite network, claiming its frontline defenses would collapse if the service were switched off.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Dutch police extradite Chinese national accused of laundering Cambodian investment scam funds
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: 44-year-old Zheng Zhao was allegedly a key money-launderer working with a group of scammers who called U.S.-based victims and urged them to invest in fictitious businesses.
articles.full_text:
Dutch police extradite Chinese national accused of laundering Cambodian investment scam funds
A Chinese national was extradited from The Netherlands and arraigned on Friday after prosecutors accused him of facilitating an investment fraud scheme through scam centers in Cambodia.
44-year-old Zheng Zhao was allegedly a key money-launderer working with a group of scammers who called U.S.-based victims and urged them to invest in fictitious businesses.
Zhao is the ninth person to be charged as part of the scheme after eight others pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.
Court documents said Zhao helped facilitate the transfer of stolen funds to a bank account at Deltec Bank in the Bahamas. Zhao converted the funds into cryptocurrency stablecoin USDT, which allowed it to be transferred to digital wallets controlled by people in Cambodia. The funds were then spread to the leaders of scam centers throughout Southeast Asia.
Zhao was charged in August 2025 and is facing up to 20 years in prison if convicted on one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. Zhao appeared in a California district court on Friday.
U.S. investigators have identified at least 174 American victims of the scheme, which saw scammers contact people on social media or through phone calls, texts and dating sites. The scammers convinced victims to invest in fake digital asset services and used fictitious screenshots alleging their investments were growing.
In total, the group transferred at least $36.9 million in victim funds to the Deltec Bank account.
ShengSheng He and Jingliang Su – two other coconspirators previously charged alongside Zhao — pleaded guilty and were sentenced last year to 51 months and 46 months in prison respectively.
Prosecutors said most of the funds were transferred to scam center leaders based in the Cambodian coastal city of Sihanoukville — a well-known haven for Chinese criminal activity.
Several of those who pleaded guilty traveled back and forth between the U.S. and Cambodia’s capital Phnom Penh, coordinating the transfer of stolen funds.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Ukraine warns hackers are exploiting Chinese-made Dahua surveillance cameras
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: CERT-UA says it has identified cases in which hackers compromised Dahua internet-connected cameras and video recorders, changed their settings and created unauthorized user accounts.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine warns hackers are exploiting Chinese-made Dahua surveillance cameras
Ukrainian government cybersecurity researchers have warned that hackers are gaining unauthorized access to surveillance cameras made by Chinese manufacturer Dahua, potentially exposing video feeds and allowing attackers to remotely control the devices.
Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA, said late last week that it had identified cases in which hackers compromised the internet-connected cameras and video recorders, changed their settings and created unauthorized user accounts.
The agency did not say how many devices had been compromised, when the attacks occurred or who was responsible. Chinese-made surveillance equipment remains widely used in Ukraine, including by government institutions and military units.
According to CERT-UA, the attackers appear to be exploiting a feature called Easy4IP, which allows users to access Dahua cameras remotely through the manufacturer's cloud service. The feature connects devices to the cloud using their serial numbers, even when the devices are protected by firewalls or cannot be accessed directly over the internet.
CERT-UA said the serial numbers follow predictable patterns, allowing hackers to guess large numbers of them and identify cameras connected to the cloud. As a result, devices with the remote access feature enabled could be vulnerable even if their serial numbers have never been publicly disclosed.
Once a device is identified, attackers can attempt to gain access by guessing weak or default passwords or exploiting security flaws in outdated firmware that allow them to bypass authentication.
The agency specifically warned about two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045, disclosed in 2021, that affect certain Dahua cameras and video recorders.
Researchers at cybersecurity firm Hunt.io reported in August that hackers had compromised more than 14,500 Dahua devices earlier in the summer, with confirmed infections concentrated in Ukraine and Russia. The attackers reportedly used similar techniques, although it remains unclear whether the incidents are connected to those described by CERT-UA.
Hunt.io told Recorded Future News that the methods described by CERT-UA closely match those used in the earlier campaign, but there is no evidence linking the attacks to the same hackers.
The servers used in the earlier campaign remain online, although researchers have found no new copies of the attackers' toolkit since July. Hunt.io cautioned that the lack of evidence does not mean the attacks have stopped, as the hackers appear to have restricted access to the files that originally exposed their operations.
The company also said that compromised cameras could remain accessible to hackers months later because malicious accounts and recovery codes can survive password changes and, on most firmware versions, factory resets. The researchers said removing the accounts is not enough to secure the devices without updating their firmware.
Dahua is one of China's largest manufacturers of video surveillance equipment, producing security cameras, recording systems and facial recognition technology.
The company has faced restrictions in the United States over national security and human rights concerns. In 2018, Congress prohibited federal agencies from procuring certain Dahua equipment, and the following year, Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist over its alleged role in the surveillance and repression of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities in China's Xinjiang region.
Surveillance risks in wartime
The warning comes amid longstanding concerns in Ukraine that surveillance cameras could be exploited by Russian intelligence services to monitor military movements and critical infrastructure.
Earlier this month, The Wall Street Journal reported that Ukraine's domestic security agency, the SBU, had identified and secured approximately 40,000 surveillance cameras since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, amid concerns that they could be used to gather military intelligence.
In January 2024, the SBU said Russian intelligence services had hacked two cameras installed on residential buildings in Kyiv and used them to monitor air defense activity and critical infrastructure. The cameras, originally installed to monitor nearby streets and parking areas, were allegedly reconfigured by Russian operatives to change their viewing angles and stream footage to YouTube.
A 2024 investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty found that approximately 24,000 cameras manufactured by Dahua and another Chinese company, Hikvision, were installed in municipal surveillance systems across Ukraine.
Ukrainian public procurement records show that government institutions and military units continued to purchase Dahua equipment in 2026 despite longstanding security concerns.
It remains unclear whether any of the devices identified in CERT-UA's latest warning belong to Ukrainian government agencies or military organizations.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Popular AI tool LiteLLM says unrevoked key allowed hackers to target users
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: LiteLLM, an open-source tool widely used by artificial intelligence developers, said a key accidentally exposed in May was behind a supply-chain attack that is believed to have hit tens of thousands of users last week.
articles.full_text:
Popular AI tool LiteLLM says unrevoked key allowed hackers to target users
LiteLLM, an open-source tool widely used by artificial intelligence developers, said Friday that a key accidentally exposed in May was behind a supply-chain attack that is believed to have hit tens of thousands of users last week.
In a root-cause analysis published Friday, the project traced the attack to the company's own mistaken exposure months before of a configuration file containing the master key to an internal tool used by LiteLLM to run AI agents.
Although the company spotted the publication at the time and removed the file, it failed to revoke the exposed key. Earlier this month, an unidentified attacker used the key to access LiteLLM’s tooling and grab an access token giving them control over all of LiteLLM’s repositories on GitHub.
According to the initial incident report, the attacker then exploited "multiple independent security controls” last week to distribute a version of the tool containing credential-harvesting malware to the software’s users.
Google-owned cloud security company Wiz said the compromised package was downloaded about 49,000 times and that the cloud credentials stolen from LiteLLM users were being tested within hours.
The malicious package remained on the Python Package Index (PyPI) for about two hours. Within about four and a half hours of it being initially uploaded, the attacker was trying out stolen login credentials for Amazon’s AWS cloud service to see which of Amazon’s AI models the accounts could access.
Wiz said this matched a pattern known as “LLMjacking,” in which criminals use stolen cloud accounts to run AI services and leave the victims with the bill. No affected organization has publicly confirmed a breach linked to the release.
According to Microsoft, the malware was designed to run whenever the Python programming language started up on an infected machine, even if the program that was being run never used LiteLLM itself.
LiteLLM warned that anyone who installed the compromised version (1.107.0) on an internet-connected computer should assume their credentials were stolen. Those entities were advised to change every password and access key that the affected computer could reach.
LiteLLM said it too was revoking tokens across its internal systems and vendor platforms.
The incident is the second supply chain compromise of LiteLLM this year. In March, attackers published malicious versions to PyPI in a campaign later linked to the TeamPCP hacking group. Australian police have since charged two men alleged to be TeamPCP members.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: FCC bans two devices with surveillance chips linked to Huawei
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market.”
articles.full_text:
FCC bans two devices with surveillance chips linked to Huawei
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Thursday said it won’t let devices made with surveillance chips manufactured by a Chinese tech firm enter the U.S. market, the first instance of such a ban following the agency’s implementation of tough new rules.
The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC said.
New rules took effect on October 13 that bans devices containing smart components made by companies on a so-called covered list, an official public directory the agency maintains under a 2019 regulation identifying video surveillance, communications and general technology products believed to threaten national security. HiSilicon was included on the list.
Before the new regulations were implemented, agency rules did not ban “otherwise lawful devices” from including component parts manufactured by covered list entities, the press release said.
“The FCC will continue to act with vigilance in protecting and promoting America’s national security,” Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that called the products potential spyware. “Video devices containing surveillance chips produced by Covered List entities pose an obvious and unacceptable risk to the nation and our people.”
Huawei did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.snippet: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.
Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.
I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.
This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing.
